newsitem.title: GERMANY: German flood-hit villagers revolt over new dike.
newsitem.headline: German flood-hit villagers revolt over new dike.

text.p: Villagers protested on Tuesday against plans to build a second flood barrier along the Oder River in the first confrontation with relief workers in flood-hit east Germany.

The incident overshadowed a much-praised operation involving thousands of soldiers and other relief workers and contrasted with a more positive mood in the region, where people expressed relief the worst of the flooding was over.
Residents in the village of Reitwein, just north of Frankfurt an der Oder, said plans to build an emergency dike there were a waste of time and efforts.

Dozens of them blocked a road for a couple of hours to stop deliveries of sand creating a tailback of about 100 German army and relief operation vehicles loaded with sand to build up the flood barriers.

"We were told that an emergency dike was needed to prevent potential disaster, we understand and support this, but this dike is stable. The main dike is the important thing," Reitwein's mayor Karl Friedrich Teitz told Berlin's InfoRadio.

Villagers argued the emergency barrier would not protect all houses from flooding. Reitwein is in the low-lying Oderbruch area which was reclaimed 250 years under Frederich the Great and is protected from the river by a series of dikes.
The row was settled when regional government officials proposed a compromise to reduce planned work on the dike.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl pledged up to 500 million marks ($268.3 million) in federal government aid to the region along the Oder River, calling floods there in the past weeks the "worst natural disaster ever faced by newly-unified Germany".
He did not specify whether it would take the form of direct government grants or available as soft loans, such as a 200-million-mark credit already announced.
Inhabitants of the flood region in other villages praised government efforts to help them so far saying these had come as a surprise to them.

"We never expected such support and we have been really impressed by the enormous efforts of the German army to secure our homes," said Eveline Krueger, 55, a resident in Ratzdorf, south of Frankfurt an der Oder.
She praised Defence Minister Volker Ruehe who promised to keep 10,000 troops, who had been securing flood barriers along the river, to stay on and help clean up villages.
"Because of this support, we have been able to feel safe at night in our beds," said Krueger, standing outside her house which was narrowly saved from flooding by the wall of army sandbags.
"It's brought people in the village closer together. Before it was every man for himself," said resident Christiane Sass.

Manfred Stolpe, premier of the flood-hit state of Brandenburg, hailed the relief effort as a token of solidarity between Germany's former communist east and the more affluent west at a special session of the lower house of parliament.

"In the seventh year after unification the German nation has passed its probation test on the Oder dikes," said Stolpe, who was once a native of the former communist country and is today one of east Germany's most popular politicians.
The Oder was swollen by the same rains that caused flooding in the Czech Republic and Poland last month claiming more than 100 lives and causing billions of dollars' worth of damage.
Germany has escaped the worst of the floods, but damage to homes, businesses and farms has been extensive.
